name: Bootstrap Project
description: Instantiate and formalize a project from concept or in-flight state to a structured, execution-ready endeavor.

narratives.name: Bootstrapping Projects From Ambiguity to Execution Readiness
narratives.description: Practice narrative describing the bootstrap journey from concept to structured endeavor.

narrativeContexts.context: Organizations initiating new projects or formalizing in-flight efforts face ambiguity across all management concerns -- unclear opportunity definition, unidentified stakeholders, undefined governance, unformed teams, and unmanaged risks. Without structured inception, projects begin execution with unstated assumptions, misaligned expectations, and insufficient readiness.

Bootstrap the project from initial concept or informal effort to a manageable, value-driven endeavor ready for structured execution. This requires simultaneously advancing all seven baseline concerns from their initial states to a level sufficient for confident transition to delivery.

Apply a coordinated set of inception activities spanning situational assessment, stakeholder mapping, inception workshops, governance establishment, team formation, backlog creation, risk identification, and readiness evaluation. These activities operate across all three focuses (Value, Solution, Endeavor) to produce a holistic bootstrap that addresses both greenfield inception and brownfield formalization paths.

An execution-ready project with documented context, validated opportunity, aligned stakeholders, articulated objectives, envisioned deliverable, authorized work, formed team, established ways of working, seeded backlog, drafted team agreements, and identified risks. The project is ready for transition to delivery and ongoing management practices.

narratives.name: Establishing Project Context Through Situational Assessment
narratives.description: How systematic context analysis prevents methodology misapplication.
citationNames: A Leader's Framework for Decision Making

narrativeContexts.context: Every project operates within an environmental setting that profoundly shapes which management approaches will succeed and which will fail. Understanding context -- domain complexity, organizational readiness, regulatory landscape, and strategic positioning -- before committing to a management approach prevents the common failure of applying inappropriate methodologies to misunderstood problems.

Planellas and Muni's survey of thirty strategic management models demonstrates that multiple analytical tools exist for each contextual concern, and the practitioner's task is selecting appropriate tools rather than defaulting to a single framework. Domain complexity classification helps teams distinguish ordered environments requiring structured approaches from complex environments requiring adaptive ones. Component evolution analysis reveals where commoditized solutions exist versus where custom development is justified. Organizational readiness assessment surfaces cultural, structural, and capability gaps that must be addressed before transformation can succeed.

When project context is made explicit through systematic analysis rather than left as unstated assumptions, teams make better decisions about governance intensity, development approach, and risk management, establishing a foundation for all subsequent bootstrap activities.

narratives.name: From Vague Need to Validated Investment Through Structured Bootstrap
narratives.description: How bootstrap activities systematically validate opportunity before execution commitment.

narrativeContexts.context: In the bootstrap context, opportunity management is the critical gate between organizational aspiration and committed investment. A project that begins without a clearly defined, validated opportunity risks consuming resources on a problem that was never properly understood or a solution that was never properly justified.

The bootstrap practice focuses on the early opportunity states -- moving from initial identification through determination to viability. Techniques such as pre-mortem analysis, assumption mapping, and structured inception workshops provide the analytical rigor needed to distinguish genuine opportunities from organizational assumptions. Both greenfield and brownfield projects require this discipline, though the specific assessments differ: greenfield projects need vision validation and scope definition, while brownfield projects need current-state assessment and technical debt evaluation.

When bootstrap activities systematically validate the opportunity before committing to full execution, organizations achieve higher project success rates and earlier identification of projects that should be deferred or cancelled, preserving investment capacity for higher-value endeavors.

narratives.name: Comprehensive Stakeholder Discovery During Project Inception
narratives.description: How systematic stakeholder discovery during bootstrap establishes the political foundation for project success.
citationNames: Toward a Theory of Stakeholder Identification and Salience

narrativeContexts.context: The bootstrap phase offers a unique and time-limited window to identify and engage stakeholders before project momentum makes course corrections costly. Stakeholders discovered during inception can shape the project's direction; stakeholders discovered during execution can only react to decisions already made.

Effective bootstrap stakeholder engagement combines multiple identification techniques -- organizational chart analysis, value chain mapping, and structured brainstorming -- to surface not only obvious sponsors and users but also hidden influencers, potential obstructors, and downstream groups who will be affected by project outcomes. Structured engagement assessment moves beyond simple identification to categorize stakeholders by influence, interest, and salience, enabling differentiated engagement strategies that allocate limited inception time to the highest-value interactions.

When stakeholder discovery and engagement are treated as a systematic discipline during bootstrap rather than an ad hoc effort, projects establish the political foundation and relationship capital needed for successful execution and adoption.

narratives.name: Translating Opportunity Into Measurable Project Targets
narratives.description: How bootstrap objective identification bridges validated opportunity and actionable project scope.

narrativeContexts.context: During bootstrap, objectives serve as the bridge between a validated opportunity and actionable project scope. Without clearly identified objectives, inception activities produce shared understanding that never converts into measurable commitments.

Bootstrap objective identification focuses on deriving goals from opportunity drivers and stakeholder needs rather than prescribing detailed requirements. The practice emphasizes establishing a primary success measure that provides focus for all subsequent planning, ensuring that the team and stakeholders share a common definition of what success looks like before committing resources to delivery. Objectives at this stage deliberately remain at the outcome level, with detailed requirements emerging during delivery practices.

When objectives are identified early with clear traceability to the opportunity and stakeholder needs, projects maintain strategic alignment throughout delivery, providing a stable reference point for scope decisions, trade-off negotiations, and progress evaluation.

narratives.name: Envisioning the Deliverable Through Greenfield and Brownfield Lenses
narratives.description: How bootstrap creates shared deliverable vision through divergent inception paths.

narrativeContexts.context: During bootstrap, the deliverable must progress from an abstract idea to a shared vision that the team, stakeholders, and governance can evaluate for feasibility and alignment. The path to this vision differs fundamentally between greenfield projects creating something new and brownfield projects formalizing or modernizing something existing.

Greenfield bootstrap focuses on vision articulation through techniques such as product vision boards and collaborative feature brainstorming, establishing the minimum viable scope that will demonstrate value with the least investment. Brownfield bootstrap focuses on documenting the current state -- inventorying existing systems, cataloguing technical debt, mapping architecture, and collecting operational knowledge from practitioners who maintain the existing deliverable. Both paths converge on a shared understanding of what the deliverable will look like and what constraints shape its development.

When the deliverable is envisioned through a structured bootstrap process, the team enters execution with a shared mental model rather than divergent assumptions, reducing costly rework and miscommunication during delivery.

narratives.name: Authorizing and Preparing Work for Confident Execution
narratives.description: How bootstrap transitions work from authorization to readiness.

narrativeContexts.context: The bootstrap practice's contribution to Work concerns the transition from authorization to readiness. Work must be formally initiated with clear mandate, then prepared through planning, estimation, and backlog creation before execution can begin with confidence.

Effective work preparation during bootstrap combines top-down governance authorization with bottom-up team planning. The project charter provides formal authorization and constraints, while story mapping and backlog creation translate the deliverable vision into executable work items. Completion criteria establish quality standards that prevent ambiguity during execution about what constitutes finished work. The bootstrap practice deliberately stops at the boundary of work preparation, leaving work execution and control to delivery practices.

When work is properly authorized and prepared during bootstrap, teams begin execution with clear mandate, realistic estimates, and a structured backlog rather than starting from an ambiguous directive that requires ongoing negotiation of scope and standards.

narratives.name: Building Teams for Bootstrap Through Deliberate Composition and Onboarding
narratives.description: How deliberate team formation during bootstrap accelerates team development.

narrativeContexts.context: Team formation during bootstrap sets the trajectory for all subsequent delivery. A team that is thoughtfully composed, properly onboarded, and given early opportunities to build trust will accelerate through development stages faster than one assembled by availability and left to self-organize without support.

Bootstrap team formation combines analytical competency mapping with deliberate culture-building. Competency requirements are derived from work complexity rather than organizational defaults, and team size is calibrated to cognitive capacity rather than budget availability alone. Structured onboarding ensures new members have tooling access, domain context, and relationship connections from day one. Early team-building activities and collaborative working agreement creation establish psychological safety that enables the candid communication essential for complex project work.

When team formation is treated as a deliberate design exercise during bootstrap rather than an administrative staffing task, projects build teams capable of sustained high performance rather than groups of individuals who must discover how to work together through trial and error.

narratives.name: Selecting and Establishing an Appropriate Project Methodology
narratives.description: How context-driven methodology selection prevents bootstrap failures.
citationNames: A Leader's Framework for Decision Making

narrativeContexts.context: The bootstrap phase must establish a way of working that fits the project's complexity, team capability, and organizational context. Premature commitment to a specific methodology without contextual assessment is a common bootstrap failure that creates friction throughout delivery.

Effective way of working establishment begins with domain complexity classification informing the selection of an appropriate development approach -- from predictive to adaptive or hybrid. The selection considers team experience, organizational culture, and governance requirements rather than defaulting to a single methodology. Once selected, the foundation is established through minimal but essential elements: work cadence, completion criteria, team ceremonies, and tooling. The principle of conscious minimalism applies -- establish what is needed to begin effective work, deferring practice refinement to the delivery phase when the team has empirical evidence of what works.

When the way of working is selected through deliberate analysis and established through minimal viable process, teams begin execution with a coherent methodology that supports their work rather than a prescriptive framework that constrains it.

narratives.name: Seeding the Backlog From Inception Workshop to Structured Inventory
narratives.description: How bootstrap converts shared understanding into actionable work items.
citationNames: The Principles of Product Development Flow

narrativeContexts.context: The bootstrap practice transitions the deliverable vision from inception artifacts into a structured, prioritized backlog that the delivery team can execute against. A well-seeded backlog converts shared understanding into actionable work items.

Backlog seeding during bootstrap combines top-down vision decomposition with bottom-up story writing workshops. The inception deck's scope and trade-off decisions inform what belongs in the backlog, while collaborative story writing ensures the team understands and owns the work items they will execute. Initial prioritization applies economic frameworks to establish delivery sequencing, and minimum viable scope identification through story mapping identifies the thinnest end-to-end slice that delivers learning or demonstrable value.

When the backlog is seeded through structured inception activities rather than unstructured brainstorming, the delivery team inherits a coherent, prioritized inventory that connects directly to stakeholder needs and the validated opportunity.

narratives.name: Establishing Explicit Social Contracts for Team Effectiveness
narratives.description: How bootstrap creates behavioral foundations for productive collaboration.

narrativeContexts.context: Team agreements transform implicit expectations into explicit commitments, preventing the misunderstandings and friction that arise when team members operate under different assumptions about how to work together.

Effective bootstrap agreement creation requires facilitated workshops where all team members contribute to defining norms rather than having agreements imposed by management. The agreements cover practical concerns -- collaboration hours, communication channels, meeting expectations -- alongside cultural commitments such as decision-making processes and conflict resolution approaches. The bootstrap practice focuses on drafting agreements that are good enough to begin work, recognizing that agreements must be tested through practice before they can be refined through retrospective reflection during delivery.

When team agreements are explicitly created during bootstrap through inclusive facilitation, teams establish the behavioral foundation that enables psychological safety and productive collaboration from the first day of execution.

narratives.name: Surfacing Project Risks Through Prospective Hindsight and Assumption Testing
narratives.description: How bootstrap risk identification overcomes optimism bias through structured techniques.

narrativeContexts.context: The bootstrap phase is the optimal time to identify project risks because team members and stakeholders have fresh perspectives unbiased by execution momentum. Risks surfaced during inception can be addressed proactively; risks discovered during execution require reactive intervention.

Bootstrap risk identification combines two complementary techniques: pre-mortem analysis, which uses prospective hindsight to surface risks that traditional brainstorming misses, and assumption mapping, which identifies the critical assumptions underlying the project's success and prioritizes them for validation. Research demonstrates that pre-mortem exercises surface significantly more risks than conventional risk brainstorming because imagining failure removes the optimism bias inherent in project planning. The combination of these techniques with comprehensive category coverage ensures that risks across technical, organizational, market, and regulatory domains are systematically surfaced.

When risk identification is conducted through structured techniques during bootstrap, projects enter execution with a comprehensive risk inventory and validation plan rather than discovering critical risks through costly failures during delivery.

narratives.name: The Project Charter as Authorization and Alignment Instrument
narratives.description: How the project charter serves dual purposes of formal authorization and shared alignment.

narrativeContexts.context: The project charter serves dual purposes during bootstrap: it provides formal authorization for the project to consume organizational resources, and it creates a shared reference document aligning all participants on purpose, scope, governance, and success criteria.

Effective project charters evolve from executive summary through comprehensive integration. The initial one-page summary enables rapid authorization, while subsequent elaboration incorporates inception workshop outputs, stakeholder analysis, and governance design. PRINCE2 emphasizes the project initiation document as the foundation for management by exception, enabling delegated authority within defined tolerances. The charter becomes a living baseline when it is maintained under version control and reviewed regularly against evolving project reality.

When the project charter is developed progressively through bootstrap activities rather than treated as a one-time administrative artifact, it serves as a continuously relevant alignment tool that supports governance decision-making throughout the project lifecycle.

narratives.name: Mapping the Environmental Landscape to Inform Project Strategy
narratives.description: How progressive context mapping creates the analytical foundation for approach tailoring.
citationNames: A Leader's Framework for Decision Making

narrativeContexts.context: The context map makes the project's environmental setting visible and actionable. Without this visualization, contextual knowledge remains distributed across individual perspectives, preventing coherent strategic decisions about project approach.

The context map evolves through progressive integration of analytical perspectives. It begins with stakeholder identification and relationship mapping, adds domain complexity classification to inform management approach selection, incorporates component evolution analysis to guide sourcing strategy, and culminates in a comprehensive view integrating organizational readiness assessment. Each layer adds decision-relevant information that shapes the project's bootstrap strategy. The variety of strategic analysis models available -- as catalogued by Planellas and Muni -- provides practitioners with choices about which analytical tools best fit their specific context.

When the context map is developed as a progressive, multi-layered artifact during bootstrap, it serves as the analytical foundation for all approach tailoring decisions and as a living reference that teams revisit when project circumstances change.

narratives.name: Collaborative Inception as the Foundation for Project Alignment
narratives.description: How inception workshops create shared alignment through collaborative exercises.

narrativeContexts.context: The inception deck is the tangible output of collaborative workshops that align stakeholders, team, and governance on what the project will deliver, what it will not deliver, and what trade-offs have been accepted. It transforms individual perspectives into shared commitments.

Effective inception workshops produce artifacts that answer the essential questions every project must resolve before execution: Why are we doing this? Who is it for? What does success look like? What are we not doing? What keeps us awake at night? Multiple workshop formats exist -- including Rasmusson's Agile Inception Deck, Caroli's Lean Inception, and custom facilitated designs -- each offering structured exercises for collaborative discovery. The choice of format matters less than the discipline of conducting the exercises with genuine stakeholder participation and documenting decisions in accessible, referable artifacts.

When inception deck artifacts are created through genuinely collaborative workshops and maintained as living references, they prevent the scope creep, misalignment, and unstated assumptions that undermine projects during delivery.

narratives.name: Progressive Backlog Development From Features to Execution-Ready Inventory
narratives.description: How progressive backlog development during bootstrap creates execution-ready delivery inventory.
citationNames: The Principles of Product Development Flow

narrativeContexts.context: The initial backlog translates the deliverable vision into structured, prioritized work items that the delivery team can plan against. Without a well-seeded backlog, the transition from inception to execution stalls as teams struggle to convert abstract vision into concrete work.

Backlog development during bootstrap follows a progressive pattern: features are first enumerated from inception outputs, then structured as work items with consistent format, then organized into a narrative story map revealing user journeys and release slicing opportunities, and finally economically prioritized using frameworks that balance value, effort, risk, and time-criticality. Story mapping is particularly valuable because it preserves the user narrative context that gets lost when work items exist only as flat prioritized lists, enabling teams to identify the minimum viable scope for first delivery.

When the backlog is progressively developed through structured bootstrap activities, the delivery team inherits a coherent, economically prioritized inventory that enables confident iteration planning from the first day of execution.

narratives.name: Building a Risk Register Through Structured Inception Techniques
narratives.description: How pre-mortem and assumption mapping seed the risk register during bootstrap.

narrativeContexts.context: The risk register is seeded during bootstrap through structured techniques designed to overcome the optimism bias that suppresses risk identification during project inception.

Pre-mortem analysis and assumption mapping are the primary bootstrap techniques for populating the risk register. Pre-mortem exercises use prospective hindsight -- imagining the project has already failed -- to surface risks that team members intuitively sense but do not articulate in conventional brainstorming. Assumption mapping complements this by identifying the beliefs underlying the project's success hypothesis and prioritizing them for validation. Together, these techniques produce a comprehensive risk inventory that covers technical, organizational, market, and regulatory categories, providing the foundation for ongoing risk management during delivery.

When the risk register is seeded through structured inception techniques rather than perfunctory risk brainstorming, projects enter execution with awareness of their critical vulnerabilities and a validation plan for their most important assumptions.

narratives.name: Evaluating Bootstrap Readiness Through Multi-Concern Assessment
narratives.description: How structured readiness assessment enables informed transition decisions.

narrativeContexts.context: The bootstrap readiness report provides the evidence-based assessment that governance needs to make an informed decision about transitioning from inception to execution. It prevents the common failure of beginning execution before the project is adequately prepared.

Readiness assessment examines all bootstrap concerns holistically rather than checking individual dimensions in isolation. Each alpha's current state is evaluated with evidence, gaps between achieved and required states are identified, and the aggregate risk profile is assessed to determine whether execution can proceed with acceptable risk. The gap remediation plan provides a structured path for addressing deficiencies, including conditional proceed criteria that allow execution to begin while specific gaps are being closed under monitoring. The progress baseline captured at transition serves as the reference point for ongoing project health monitoring during delivery.

When readiness is assessed through structured multi-concern evaluation rather than subjective confidence, organizations make better proceed/defer/cancel decisions and establish a baseline for tracking project health throughout execution.

activities.name: Conduct Situational Assessment
activities.description: Analyze the project's environmental setting, complexity profile, and contextual constraints.

narratives.name: Situational Assessment for Project Context
narratives.description: How systematic environmental analysis informs project approach decisions.
citationNames: A Leader's Framework for Decision Making

narrativeContexts.context: Situational assessment establishes the project's environmental context, enabling informed decisions about management approach, governance intensity, and risk profile before execution commitments are made.

Begin with environmental scanning to identify major external factors, then apply domain complexity classification to understand the nature of the work, followed by component evolution analysis to inform sourcing and investment decisions. Multiple analytical models exist for each concern -- select the ones most appropriate to the project's domain and organizational context. Validate findings with stakeholders who have operational knowledge of the environment.

Defaulting to a single analytical framework without considering alternatives. Treating situational assessment as a one-time exercise rather than a progressive analysis. Allowing executive assumptions about project context to substitute for systematic investigation.

activities.name: Facilitate Inception Workshop
activities.description: Conduct collaborative visioning workshop producing shared understanding of purpose, scope, trade-offs, and priorities.

narratives.name: Facilitating Collaborative Inception for Project Alignment
narratives.description: How inception workshops create shared alignment through collaborative exercises.

narrativeContexts.context: The inception workshop is the centerpiece bootstrap activity, producing shared alignment on project purpose, scope, trade-offs, and priorities through collaborative exercises that engage both the delivery team and key stakeholders.

Select an appropriate workshop format based on project context and facilitator experience. Conduct exercises that address vision, scope boundaries, trade-off decisions, stakeholder identification, and risk awareness. Ensure genuine participation from decision-makers, not just proxies. Document outputs in accessible artifacts that serve as living references. Multiple workshop formats exist for each inception concern; the facilitator should select exercises that fit the project's complexity and the participants' experience level.

Conducting inception exercises with too few stakeholders or without decision-making authority present. Treating inception as a one-day event rather than a structured series of collaborative sessions. Allowing the loudest voice to dominate rather than using facilitation techniques that ensure all perspectives are heard.

activities.name: Map Stakeholder Landscape
activities.description: Systematically identify stakeholders, analyze influence dynamics, and design engagement strategies.

narratives.name: Systematic Stakeholder Discovery and Engagement Design
narratives.description: How structured stakeholder mapping creates the political foundation for project success.
citationNames: Toward a Theory of Stakeholder Identification and Salience

narrativeContexts.context: Stakeholder landscape mapping systematically identifies all groups affected by or involved in the project, analyzes their influence dynamics, and designs differentiated engagement strategies that allocate limited inception time to highest-value interactions.

Begin with systematic identification using organizational analysis, value chain mapping, and brainstorming to surface stakeholders beyond the obvious. Apply structured analysis techniques to categorize stakeholders by influence, interest, and salience. Design differentiated engagement strategies matching each segment's analysis results. Create visual stakeholder maps that make the landscape accessible to the entire team.

Identifying only supporters and ignoring potential obstructors. Treating stakeholder mapping as a document exercise rather than a relationship-building activity. Failing to update the stakeholder landscape as the project evolves and new groups emerge.

narratives.name: Calibrating Governance to Project Complexity
narratives.description: How governance framework establishment creates appropriate autonomy with accountability.

narrativeContexts.context: Governance framework establishment creates the decision-making structures and accountability mechanisms that enable the project to operate with appropriate autonomy while maintaining organizational alignment and control.

Calibrate governance intensity to project complexity and risk. Define decision-making authority using structured decision frameworks that clarify who recommends, who inputs, and who decides for each decision type. Establish escalation paths with clear triggers and response timeframes. Document authority boundaries that enable team autonomy within defined tolerances. The governance framework should be the minimum effective structure, avoiding bureaucratic overhead that slows decision-making without adding value.

Applying uniform governance regardless of project complexity. Creating governance structures that require executive involvement in operational decisions. Failing to define escalation triggers, leaving the team unsure when to escalate versus when to decide independently.

activities.name: Assess Current State (Brownfield)
activities.description: Document existing system state including architecture, technical debt, capability maturity, and gaps.

narratives.name: Documenting the Existing Landscape for Brownfield Projects
narratives.description: How current-state assessment reveals the true landscape of existing systems and technical debt.

narrativeContexts.context: Brownfield assessment documents the existing state of systems, processes, and capabilities that the project will modify, modernize, or formalize, providing the baseline understanding needed for informed planning.

Inventory existing applications, databases, services, and integrations to create a comprehensive system catalog. Document current architecture through component and deployment diagrams. Assess technical debt by categorizing existing issues and quantifying remediation effort. Interview operational stakeholders to capture institutional knowledge, pain points, and workarounds not documented elsewhere. Catalogue operational runbooks and documentation to establish the knowledge baseline.

Relying solely on documentation without interviewing practitioners who maintain the systems. Underestimating technical debt by cataloguing only visible issues. Treating brownfield assessment as optional when the project involves existing systems.

activities.name: Form and Onboard Team
activities.description: Assemble team with skill-based assignment, execute structured onboarding, and establish communication channels.

narratives.name: Deliberate Team Composition and Structured Onboarding
narratives.description: How deliberate team formation accelerates team development stages.

narrativeContexts.context: Team formation and onboarding transforms a set of assigned individuals into a functioning team with shared context, established communication, and the initial trust needed for collaborative work.

Assign individuals to roles based on competency match against work requirements. Execute structured onboarding covering tooling access, domain context, codebase orientation, and key relationship introductions. Conduct initial team-building activities to establish rapport and begin building psychological safety. Configure physical or virtual workspace with visibility into work progress. Establish communication channels and meeting cadence before execution begins.

Staffing by availability rather than competency match. Skipping structured onboarding and expecting new members to self-orient. Neglecting team-building activities under time pressure, sacrificing team cohesion for perceived speed.

activities.name: Define Ways of Working
activities.description: Select development approach, establish ceremony cadence, define completion criteria, and configure tooling.

narratives.name: Context-Driven Methodology Selection and Establishment
narratives.description: How minimal viable process establishment creates a coherent foundation for delivery.
citationNames: A Leader's Framework for Decision Making

narrativeContexts.context: Defining ways of working establishes the minimal effective process that the team needs to begin execution, including development approach, work cadence, quality standards, and tooling.

Select the development approach informed by domain complexity classification and team experience. Establish iteration cadence appropriate to the project context. Define completion criteria specifying minimum quality standards. Configure ceremony schedule with formats appropriate to team size and distribution. Provision tooling and grant access. Apply conscious minimalism -- establish what is needed to begin, deferring refinement to delivery when empirical evidence is available.

Over-engineering the process before the team has experience with the work. Selecting a methodology based on organizational preference rather than project context analysis. Treating process definition as permanent rather than an initial hypothesis to be validated through practice.

activities.name: Conduct Pre-Mortem Analysis
activities.description: Facilitate pre-mortem exercise where team imagines project failure and identifies causes, surfacing risks that conventional brainstorming misses.

narratives.name: Using Prospective Hindsight to Surface Hidden Risks
narratives.description: How pre-mortem analysis overcomes optimism bias in risk identification.

narrativeContexts.context: Pre-mortem analysis uses prospective hindsight to surface project risks that conventional brainstorming techniques miss, producing a more comprehensive risk inventory by overcoming optimism bias inherent in project planning.

Ask the team to imagine the project has failed spectacularly, then individually list all the reasons why. Use individual silent brainstorming before group discussion to prevent groupthink and anchoring. Consolidate, categorize, and prioritize the identified risks. Integrate results into the risk register and inception deck risk artifacts. This technique surfaces risks that team members intuitively sense but would not raise in conventional risk identification sessions.

Conducting the pre-mortem with only optimistic participants who cannot imagine failure. Allowing group discussion to dominate individual reflection, suppressing minority viewpoints. Generating a risk list without follow-through on assessment and mitigation planning.

activities.name: Map Assumptions for Validation
activities.description: Identify critical assumptions underlying project success and plot them by importance versus evidence to prioritize validation.

narratives.name: Prioritizing Assumptions for Validation Through Structured Mapping
narratives.description: How assumption mapping identifies the most critical beliefs requiring evidence.

narrativeContexts.context: Assumption mapping identifies the beliefs underlying the project's success hypothesis and prioritizes them for validation, ensuring that the most critical and least-evidenced assumptions receive attention before significant resources are committed.

Facilitate a session where the team identifies all assumptions underlying the project's expected success. Plot each assumption on a two-dimensional matrix of importance to success versus strength of supporting evidence. Assumptions that are highly important but poorly evidenced are the highest-priority candidates for validation experiments. Design lightweight validation approaches for the top assumptions and incorporate them into early delivery planning.

Confusing assumptions with risks -- assumptions are beliefs about things that must be true, while risks are things that might go wrong. Identifying assumptions at too high a level of abstraction to be validatable. Mapping assumptions without committing to validation experiments.

activities.name: Create User Story Map
activities.description: Organize backlog into narrative structure showing user journey backbone, story details, and release slicing.

narratives.name: Narrative-Structured Backlog Organization Through Story Mapping
narratives.description: How story mapping preserves user journey context while enabling release slicing.

narrativeContexts.context: User story mapping transforms a flat list of work items into a narrative-structured map that preserves user journey context, reveals release slicing opportunities, and identifies the minimum viable scope for first delivery.

Identify the major user activities forming the narrative backbone and sequence them left to right. Break each backbone activity into detailed story items arranged vertically by priority. Draw horizontal lines to define release slices, each representing a coherent, deliverable increment. Identify the thinnest end-to-end slice as the minimum viable scope. Use the story map to validate scope coverage against objectives and identify missing capabilities.

Creating a story map without genuine user perspective input. Treating the map as a one-time exercise rather than a living artifact that evolves with understanding. Defining release slices that are technically complete but do not deliver recognizable user value.

activities.name: Facilitate Working Agreements Workshop
activities.description: Guide team through collaborative creation of explicit social contracts covering collaboration, communication, and conflict resolution.

narratives.name: Creating Explicit Social Contracts Through Facilitated Workshops
narratives.description: How inclusive facilitation creates behavioral norms before execution pressures test team cohesion.

narrativeContexts.context: The working agreements workshop creates explicit social contracts that define how team members will interact, make decisions, and resolve disagreements, establishing behavioral norms before execution pressures test team cohesion.

Facilitate a structured session where all team members contribute to brainstorming, discussing, and agreeing on working norms. Cover collaboration hours, communication channel purposes, meeting expectations, decision-making processes, and conflict resolution approaches. Ensure all voices are included through techniques that prevent dominant personality bias. Document agreements in an accessible, visible location that the team can reference daily.

Allowing management to dictate agreements rather than facilitating team co-creation. Creating overly detailed agreements that become administrative burden. Failing to designate a time for reviewing and evolving agreements as the team matures.

activities.name: Prioritize Backlog Using Economic Framework
activities.description: Apply weighted prioritization balancing business value, effort, risk, and time-criticality for economically sound delivery sequence.

narratives.name: Applying Economic Thinking to Backlog Prioritization
narratives.description: How multi-factor economic prioritization maximizes value delivery per unit of investment.
citationNames: The Principles of Product Development Flow

narrativeContexts.context: Economic backlog prioritization establishes delivery sequencing that maximizes value delivery per unit of investment by balancing multiple factors beyond simple business value ranking.

Apply a weighted prioritization framework that considers business value, implementation effort, risk reduction, and time-criticality (cost of delay). Engage both the product owner and key stakeholders in priority discussions to ensure diverse perspectives inform sequencing. Document the rationale for priority decisions to enable future re-evaluation as circumstances change. The choice of specific prioritization technique matters less than the discipline of applying economic thinking to delivery sequencing.

Prioritizing by business value alone without considering implementation dependencies and risk. Allowing the highest-paid person's opinion to override economic analysis. Re-prioritizing so frequently that the team cannot establish stable iteration commitments.

activities.name: Evaluate Bootstrap Readiness
activities.description: Assess project readiness to transition from inception to delivery, identify gaps, and make informed proceed/defer/cancel decision.

narratives.name: Evidence-Based Readiness Assessment for Informed Transition Decisions
narratives.description: How multi-concern readiness evaluation enables informed proceed/defer/cancel decisions.

narrativeContexts.context: Bootstrap readiness evaluation provides the evidence-based assessment that governance needs to make an informed proceed/defer/cancel decision about transitioning from inception to structured execution.

Assess each bootstrap concern (all eleven alphas) against expected minimum states for execution readiness. Identify gaps between achieved and required states with evidence. Calculate aggregate risk profile considering the combined effect of readiness gaps. Produce a recommendation with clear rationale. For gaps that do not prevent execution, define conditional proceed criteria with monitoring mechanisms. Establish the readiness assessment as a progress baseline for ongoing health tracking.

Treating readiness as binary (ready/not ready) rather than acknowledging conditional readiness with managed gaps. Allowing schedule pressure to bypass readiness assessment. Evaluating individual concerns in isolation without assessing the aggregate risk profile of combined gaps.

patterns.name: Project Bootstrap Journey
patterns.description: End-to-end lifecycle for bootstrapping a project from concept to execution-ready endeavor.

narratives.name: The Bootstrap Transformation From Ambiguity to Readiness
narratives.description: How the bootstrap journey transforms organizational aspiration into execution-ready managed endeavor.

narrativeContexts.context: Organizations frequently initiate projects without structured inception, relying on informal understanding, assumed alignment, and untested assumptions. The bootstrap journey addresses this gap by providing a systematic path from ambiguous concept to execution-ready managed endeavor.

A catalyst -- executive mandate, strategic imperative, or operational necessity -- drives systematic inception or formalization. The call requires structured discovery, stakeholder alignment, and readiness assessment before resources are committed to execution.

The bootstrap team must navigate competing stakeholder priorities, reconcile greenfield ambitions with brownfield realities, surface uncomfortable risks through pre-mortem analysis, and build team cohesion under time pressure. The most challenging moments arise when analysis reveals that the opportunity is weaker than assumed or that organizational readiness is insufficient for the desired approach.

The project emerges from bootstrap as a transformed endeavor -- governance authorized, team formed and collaborating, ways of working established and in use, backlog refined and prioritized, risks assessed and managed, and context fully interpreted. The organization gains a reusable bootstrap pattern that improves future project initiation.

The project exists as an idea, directive, or informal effort that has not been systematically incepted. Context is implicit, stakeholders are unengaged in structured ways, the approach is undefined, and risks are unexamined. Ambiguity, assumption, and informal management characterize the starting position.

patternViews.name: Vision and Context Discovery
patternViews.description: Establish shared vision and map environmental context.

narrativeContexts.context: A catalyst -- executive mandate, strategic imperative, or operational necessity -- drives systematic inception or formalization. The team begins structured discovery through situational assessment, stakeholder mapping, and inception workshops, replacing informal assumptions with documented, validated understanding. For brownfield projects, current-state assessment reveals the true landscape of existing systems, debt, and operational knowledge.

patternViews.name: Structure and Readiness Building
patternViews.description: Establish governance, form team, define process, seed backlog, identify risks.

narrativeContexts.context: The team navigates the most intensive phase of bootstrap, simultaneously establishing governance structures, forming and onboarding the team, defining ways of working, creating the initial backlog, identifying risks through pre-mortem and assumption mapping, and building team agreements. Competing priorities, stakeholder politics, and the tension between thoroughness and urgency create the ordeal that tests the team's cohesion and the organization's commitment to structured inception.

patternViews.name: Validation and Readiness
patternViews.description: Assess readiness and authorize transition to execution.

narrativeContexts.context: The project emerges from bootstrap as a transformed endeavor -- governance authorized, team formed and collaborating, ways of working established and in use, backlog refined and prioritized, risks assessed and managed, and context fully interpreted. The readiness evaluation confirms that the project has achieved sufficient maturity across all concerns to transition confidently from inception to structured delivery execution. Lessons from the bootstrap experience improve future project initiation.
